result: All three central vestibular neuron classes (PVP, EH, VO) display a wide range of resting discharge variability distributed along a continuum, with PVP neurons showing significantly lower CV values than EH neurons, and variability being independent of mean firing rate.
evaluation: Claims C13, C22, C27-C31 provide converging evidence from experimental measurements showing unimodal CV distributions across all neuron classes, with appropriate statistical tests (ANOVA with Bonferroni correction) demonstrating differences between PVP and EH neurons (p<0.03) and lack of correlation between firing rate and CV. The sample sizes (PVP N=20, EH N=15, VO N=17) are reasonable for this type of study.

result: Neurons with high resting discharge variability display temporal whitening (frequency-independent power spectra), while neurons with low variability do not whiten but instead show power spectra that decay with frequency similar to the stimulus. This relationship between variability and whitening is universal across neuron classes and independent of firing rate.
evaluation: Claims C14-C15, C32-C43 demonstrate a consistent relationship between CV and temporal whitening across all neuron classes, supported by power spectral analysis (C32-C33), independence from firing rate (C35-C36), and validated by both simple and linear-nonlinear cascade models (C39-C41) with excellent agreement (p>0.34 for all comparisons). The use of Poisson confidence intervals and multiple validation approaches strengthens these findings.

result: Low variability neurons transmit more information in absolute terms (higher mutual information and SNR) than high variability neurons, but high variability neurons are more optimal in that their mutual information approaches the theoretical maximum for their level of variability.
evaluation: Claims C44-C49 provide a coherent information-theoretic analysis showing that while low variability neurons have higher SNR and mutual information rates (C45-C47), high variability neurons achieve higher optimality of coding (C48). This establishes the trade-off between information transmission and coding optimality, with appropriate statistical support (significant correlations with CV).

result: Neurons with lower variability more faithfully encode the detailed time course of naturalistic stimuli as quantified by coding fraction (CF), with PVP neurons showing the highest CF values. This faithful encoding is independent of firing rate but strongly dependent on CV, establishing a trade-off between faithful encoding and temporal whitening.
evaluation: Claims C50-C57 demonstrate strong negative correlations between CF and CV (R=-0.53, p=10^-4 for all data; R=-0.51, p=0.02 for PVP), with appropriate controls showing independence from firing rate (C51-C52). The linear stimulus reconstruction methodology is well-established, and the finding that PVP neurons have the highest CF (C55) is statistically supported (ANOVA, p=4.5×10^-4).

result: Faithful stimulus encoding by low variability PVP neurons is necessary to generate compensatory VOR eye movements during naturalistic self-motion, as demonstrated by modeling showing better agreement between predicted and actual eye movements when using low variability neuron inputs (matching index negatively correlated with CV: R=-0.64, p=2.4×10^-3).
evaluation: Claims C5, C58-C64, C69-C70 use well-established VOR pathway models to demonstrate that low variability neurons better predict actual eye movements. The modeling approach is appropriate, with VOR gains approaching unity (C58) validating the behavioral measurements. The negative correlation between matching index and CV (C60) and superior performance of low variability neuron pairs (C62) provide converging evidence. Similar results for EH neurons (C63) strengthen the conclusion.

result: The short latency of VOR pathways (5 ms from PVP neurons to extraocular motoneurons) requires faithful encoding rather than temporal whitening because temporal whitening requires filtering and longer integration times incompatible with rapid feedforward control.
evaluation: Claims C73-C76 provide a mechanistic explanation for why faithful encoding is necessary for VOR generation, based on established knowledge about VOR pathway dynamics (C71-C72, supported by citations to Robinson 1981, Sylvestre and Cullen 1999, Huterer and Cullen 2002). The reasoning is logically sound: the 5 ms latency constraint is incompatible with the filtering required for decoding temporally whitened signals.

result: EH neurons, which mediate VOR adaptation and motor learning, show the least faithful encoding and display temporal whitening during naturalistic stimulation. The authors hypothesize that larger integration time windows needed to decode temporally whitened signals may be beneficial for VOR adaptation and motor learning.
evaluation: Claims C81-C83 are supported by experimental data showing EH neurons have the lowest CF values and display temporal whitening. However, C84 is explicitly speculative ("We hypothesize...") with no experimental validation. The functional interpretation for why temporal whitening would benefit motor learning lacks supporting evidence and remains an untested hypothesis requiring future work.

result: The majority of VO neurons display high variability and temporal whitening, which may be functionally advantageous for vestibulo-spinal reflexes by providing enhanced population-level information through synchrony induced by spike timing precision/phase locking inherited from irregular afferents.
evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by experimental data showing the distribution of variability in VO neurons. However, C88, C94, and C95 are explicitly speculative ("We speculate...", "We hypothesize...", "we propose..."). While C91-C93 cite prior work on afferent properties, the proposed mechanism linking temporal whitening to enhanced vestibulo-spinal reflex control through population synchrony lacks direct experimental validation in this study.

result: The subset of VO neurons with low variability that faithfully encode stimulus time course may preferentially project to thalamus to provide information for self-motion perception and spatial orientation.
evaluation: Claim C97 is explicitly speculative ("One possibility is...") without experimental validation. While C96 establishes that VO neurons project to thalamus (supported by citations), the proposed differential projection pattern based on variability is purely hypothetical. The authors acknowledge that anatomical studies identifying post-synaptic targets of individual VO neurons are needed to test this hypothesis.

result: The continuum of variability in central neurons (unlike the bimodal distribution in afferents) may arise from different amounts of feedforward input from regular and irregular afferents, differences in intrinsic neuronal properties, and/or central inputs from cortical, cerebellar, and brainstem structures.
evaluation: Claim C103 is supported by experimental data showing unimodal CV distributions and citation to prior work on afferents. However, C104, C105, and C107 are explicitly speculative ("one possibility...", "Another possibility...", "likely contribute...") without experimental validation. While C106 and C108 cite prior work establishing these inputs exist, the manuscript provides no direct evidence linking any of these mechanisms to the observed variability differences.

result: Despite the VOR showing remarkable linearity while PVP neurons and extraocular motoneurons display substantial nonlinearities, PVP neurons performing temporal whitening may contribute to compensating motoneuron nonlinearities during higher amplitude stimuli.
evaluation: Claims C77-C79 cite prior work establishing the paradox of linear VOR behavior despite nonlinear components. However, C80 is explicitly speculative ("It is further conceivable...") and applies only to "higher amplitude stimuli than the ones considered in the present study." This hypothesis is not tested and would require experiments with higher amplitude stimuli to validate.

result: The high input SNR from vestibular afferents (which display low trial-to-trial variability during naturalistic stimulation) to central neurons justifies the assumption that temporal whitening represents optimal coding according to information theory, rather than alternative optimal coding strategies based on noise filtering.
evaluation: Claims C98-C99 cite theoretical work (van Hateren 1992a,b; Rieke et al. 1996) establishing that temporal whitening is optimal for high input SNR while noise filtering is optimal for low input SNR. Claims C100-C102 cite prior work (Sadeghi et al. 2007, Jamali et al. 2016, Mitchell et al. 2018) showing that vestibular afferents have low trial-to-trial variability during naturalistic stimulation, supporting the inference in C101 that input SNR is high. This provides appropriate theoretical justification for the optimality interpretation.

result: Single-unit recordings from 52 neurons (PVP N=20, EH N=15, VO N=17) in two macaque monkeys were obtained using standard methodology, with neuronal sensitivities agreeing with previously published values and appropriate ethical approval.
evaluation: Claims C17-C20 describe the experimental dataset and methodology, with C18-C19 citing standard classification methods (Cullen 2012) and showing agreement with prior work (Roy and Cullen 2002, 2003; Massot et al. 2011; Mitchell et al. 2018). C109-C110 document ethical approval. The sample sizes are reasonable for this type of neurophysiology study, though relatively modest for some statistical comparisons (particularly EH neurons with N=15).

result: Prior work has established that VO neurons mediate vestibulo-spinal reflexes and self-motion perception, and optimally encode naturalistic self-motion through temporal whitening.
evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C8 appropriately cite prior work (Mitchell et al. 2018; Abzug et al. 1974; Shinoda et al. 1988; Gdowski and McCrea 1999; Meng et al. 2007; Marlinski and McCrea 2009; Carriot et al. 2014, 2017) establishing the background for the current study. These are literature claims rather than new findings.

result: Prior work has established the organization and functions of vestibular nuclei neurons, including that PVP neurons mediate the VOR, EH neurons mediate VOR adaptation, the VOR stabilizes gaze, and trial-to-trial variability is determined by resting discharge variability.
evaluation: Claims C2, C9-C12, C21, C85 appropriately cite prior work establishing background knowledge about vestibular system organization and function (Lisberger 1984, 1994; Lisberger et al. 1994; Ramachandran and Lisberger 2008; Goldberg et al. 2012; Sadeghi et al. 2007; Massot et al. 2011; Jamali et al. 2013; Mitchell et al. 2018; Abzug et al. 1974; Shinoda et al. 1988; Gdowski and McCrea 1999; Meng et al. 2007; Marlinski and McCrea 2009). These are literature claims providing context.
